solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Prize winner, finally official

parts.note: to prize something is to treasure it; as a noun, a prize is a treasure

indicators.note: 'finally' points at what comes at the very end, so only the closing letter of 'winner' is used

explanation.surface: An awards announcement: the prize winner, confirmed at last as official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prize winner' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'Prize' is TREASURE and 'winner' only lends its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the treasurer is the officer of a club or society who keeps its accounts.

clue.text: Tortilla stuffed with beans, regularly lacking sauce

parts.note: a taco is a folded filled tortilla

indicators.note: lacking letters at regular intervals: every second letter of 'beans' goes, keeping B, A, S

parts.note: BeAnS with the even letters dropped

explanation.surface: A lunch order: a bean taco, hold the sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface says the taco has no sauce, yet the sauce is the answer: TA(BAS)CO.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tabasco is a brand of hot chilli sauce from Louisiana.

clue.text: Wide player of little consequence

definitions.meaning: a cricket term: a ball bowled out of the batsman's reach, which gives away a run not scored off the bat
a performer with no lines, a face in a film's crowd scene

explanation.surface: A put-down of a sportsman who plays out wide and does little.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a wide is one of the extras, runs added to the score that no batsman hit; a film EXTRA is the crowd-scene player.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a wide is a kind of extra in cricket scoring, and an extra is a minor film actor.

clue.text: A sullen art, playing a comedian

indicators.note: to play with something is to move it around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sulky performance style, as if someone were acting glum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing a comedian' looks like an actor taking a role; 'playing' works on the words before it instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Stan Laurel was the thin half of the comedy double act Laurel and Hardy.

clue.text: Output of a cold, curious, absorbing man

indicators.note: something absorbing soaks another thing up into itself

explanation.surface: A strange man catching a cold and what comes out of his nose.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM as 'odd' is old-fashioned British slang (a rum do). R(HE)UM.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: rheum is the watery discharge from the nose and eyes that a cold produces.

clue.text: Meat cooked in pan with grouse

parts.note: to pan a show is to roast it, criticise it harshly
grouse and beef both mean complain

explanation.surface: A recipe: meat cooked in a pan with grouse, the game bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pan' and 'grouse' look like a cooking pot and a bird; both are verbs of complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the dish is a joint of meat cooked in the oven, the traditional British Sunday lunch.

clue.text: Hybrid Ford put out
When caught, children surrender

indicators.note: to catch a remark is to hear it, so the word is taken by sound

explanation.surface: Children who give themselves up once they are caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' here is heard, not captured, and SEED as children is biblical (Abraham's seed).
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to cede territory or a point is to surrender it.

clue.text: Elaborate about peeled figs I found

indicators.note: a peeled fruit has lost its skin, so 'figs' loses its outside letters

parts.note: fIGs without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone describing, at length, some peeled figs they came across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' is the verb to set up, not the past of find. OR(IG + I)NATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to found a movement is to originate it, to bring it into being.

clue.text: Being overheard is unnerving for leaders

indicators.note: what is overheard reaches you by ear, so the words are taken by sound

explanation.surface: Being eavesdropped on is unsettling for people in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: SHEIKHS has two pronunciations; the one needed rhymes with 'makes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sheikh is an Arab leader, the head of a tribe, family or state.

clue.text: Save a singer from massacre

indicators.note: saving someone from a place takes them out of it

explanation.surface: A plea to rescue a performer from a slaughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' is the definition in its sense 'except', and it also sets up the rescue in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: save and but both mean except, as in all save one, all but one.

clue.text: Poem by a Northern diner, drunk on beer

definitions.note: Strictly an alexandrine is a verse line rather than a whole poem.

indicators.note: someone drunk is all over the place, so the letters of 'diner' are jumbled
in an across answer, what is on the beer comes after it

parts.note: by = times, the multiplication sign X, as in 3 by 4

explanation.surface: Verse written by a northern diner who has had too much beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like authorship but is the X of 3 by 4.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose sense: an alexandrine is a twelve-syllable line of verse, the metre of classical French poetry.

clue.text: Tie-wearing British like us, with The Times

indicators.note: a word wearing another has it on, round itself

parts.note: a chess stalemate is a tie, a draw

explanation.surface: A British gent in a tie, one of us, reading The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Us' is the newspaper printing the clue: The Sunday Times and The Times share an owner. STA(B)LEMATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: stablemates share a stable or owner, as the two Times papers do.

clue.text: Founder of a little business in Kent

indicators.note: only a little of the phrase is used, a short stretch from inside it

explanation.surface: The person who started a small firm in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founder' looks like a person who starts a business; it is the verb, as a ship founders. Kent is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb sense: a ship that founders fills with water and goes down.

clue.text: Anger badly managed on the whole

indicators.note: something badly managed ends up in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A verdict that, overall, someone handles their temper poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' does double duty: its letters are fodder and it helps signal the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: by and large means generally, taking everything into account.

clue.text: Surrey, one-handed, casually making a century

indicators.note: done casually is done without order or care, so the letters are thrown together

explanation.surface: A Surrey cricketer batting one-handed and casually scoring a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is an English county with a cricket team, and in cricket a century is a hundred runs; here it is a span of time.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition of time: a century is a period of a hundred years.

clue.text: Vehicle, say, in dash from the South

indicators.note: a down answer normally reads from the north; from the south it reads upwards, reversed

parts.note: to dash is to race; reversed to ECAR

explanation.surface: A car making a dash north from the south of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' but is the verb, state. E(STATE)CAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an estate car, a station wagon in American English, is a type of vehicle.

clue.text: Feeling uneasy, one visits Dr Psycho anyhow

indicators.note: a visitor goes into a place, so I joins the doctor's letters
done anyhow is done carelessly, in no order, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A patient, anxious, going to see a scary-sounding doctor anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a nervous patient; 'Dr Psycho' is simply the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dysphoric means in a state of unease or dissatisfaction, the opposite of euphoric.

clue.text: What could make nettin' and post to frame goals

definitions.meaning: the six letters of a word meaning purpose rearrange to spell NETTIN
post = mail, written to frame, set out, what you aim to do

explanation.surface: Football talk: what the netting and posts that frame the goals are made of.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: the letters of the word INTENT could make NETTIN. The goals and posts are not football at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal document: a letter of intent sets out in writing what a party means to do.

clue.text: Part of the ear heard noise unrefined

indicators.note: what is heard is taken by sound, so the two words are said aloud together

parts.note: a row is a din, rhyming with cow

explanation.surface: Some part of someone's ear picked up a crude noise.
explanation.walkthrough: Say LOBE ROW quickly and it is LOW BROW: the B slides from the first word to the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lowbrow means lacking intellectual or cultural refinement.

clue.text: Opening rejected by play's author

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back
by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: a slot is an opening; reversed to TOLS

explanation.surface: A playwright turning down an opening night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play's author' looks like one phrase, a dramatist; the apostrophe-s is 'is', linking wordplay to 'author'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Leo Tolstoy was the Russian author of War and Peace.

clue.text: Wife worried about large insect

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way

parts.note: as in 'what's eating you?': ate = worried; reversed to ETA

explanation.surface: A wife fretting about a big bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' but turns ATE round.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the weta is a giant cricket-like insect of New Zealand, among the heaviest in the world.

clue.text: Maximum measure of digital protection?

parts.note: the surface wants computer security; the setter means a guard for a digit, a finger, when sewing
as much as that guard can hold when filled to the brim

explanation.surface: A question about the most security a computer system can have.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital protection' sounds like cybersecurity; it is a thimble on a finger, and a THIMBLEFUL is a tiny amount.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: the most a thimble can hold is a thimbleful, so the grand 'maximum' is in fact a very small quantity.

clue.text: Something fruity produced by male. Musk?

explanation.surface: A man's fragrance with a fruity note, perhaps a musk scent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musk' looks like a perfume ingredient but is Elon Musk. There is also a musk melon.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the melon is a large, sweet, juicy fruit, so 'something fruity' covers it.

clue.text: Frequency with which a philosopher brought up a goddess

indicators.note: brought up means raised, so in a down answer the name is read upwards

parts.note: A. J. Ayer, the British philosopher; reversed to REYA

explanation.surface: How often a philosopher raised the subject of a goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: A. J. Ayer was a 20th-century British philosopher, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Freya is the Norse goddess of love and fertility.

clue.text: Vessels blowing bass hooters?

indicators.note: to blow a chance or money is to lose it

explanation.surface: Ships sounding deep horns, their foghorns booming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooters' looks like horns; it is birds that hoot.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful coinage: the birds are named by their call, the hoot, so they are the hooters of the night.

clue.text: Silly brawl with old biker about Aussie singer

indicators.note: something silly is senseless and out of order, so the letters of 'brawl' are jumbled

parts.note: rockers were 1960s British bikers, rivals of the mods

explanation.surface: A pointless fight between an ageing biker and an Australian pop star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aussie singer' sounds like a pop star but is a bird. ROCK(WARBL)ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the rock warbler is a small songbird found only in New South Wales, Australia.

clue.text: One's seen in ponds, close to the banks in fact

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so the last letter of 'the' is taken
a river's banks are its two edges, so only the outside letters of 'fact' are kept

explanation.surface: A pond creature seen near the banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to the banks' reads as 'near the shore'; it splits into 'close to the' and 'banks in fact'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an eft is a newt, especially a young one, and newts live in ponds.

clue.text: Weapon's initial thrust forward produces angry talk

indicators.note: a thrust pushes something ahead, so the first letter is shoved on to the far end

parts.note: a sword is a weapon; its S moves to the end

explanation.surface: A swordsman's first lunge sparks a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrust' belongs to swordplay in the surface; in the wordplay it just pushes a letter along.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to have words with someone is to argue with them.

clue.text: Extremely noteworthy cryptic with a recent anniversary

indicators.note: take the extremes, the two ends, of 'noteworthy'
something cryptic is puzzling and obscure, so the letters are disguised by rearranging

explanation.surface: A remarkable crossword marking a recent anniversary.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue celebrates its own crossword series reaching a hundred years; 'cryptic' looks like the puzzle but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific kind: a centenary is the hundredth anniversary of an event.
